styleWhy: The video is about words, so the words themselves are the picture: each one lands huge, splits into its Chinese roots, and the wrong guess about it gets struck through.

copy.idea: Four everyday English words (ketchup, tycoon, typhoon, kowtow) were shaped by Chinese: three come from it, and it may have shaped the fourth (typhoon). Each one hides a surprising original meaning.
copy.hook: You speak a little Chinese already. Four everyday English words were shaped by it.
copy.body:
Ketchup: it started as a fish sauce. Merriam-Webster traces it, directly or via Malay 'kecap' ('fish sauce'), to Southern Min (Hokkien) 'kê-chiap': 'salted or pickled fish' + 'juice'. Today's ketchup is usually made from tomatoes.

Tycoon: the Chinese 大君 (Mandarin 'dà jūn'), 'great' + 'lord', reached English through the Japanese 'taikun', a title used for the shogun.

Typhoon: mainly from the Arabic 'tufan', shaped by the Greek storm monster Typhon. The Cantonese 'tai fung', 'a great wind', may have shaped it too.

Kowtow: from the Chinese 叩頭 (k'o-t'ou), literally 'knock' + 'head', meaning to bow until your forehead touches the ground.

Four words, one language in their story. Which one surprised you?

facts.text: Ketchup: “borrowed, directly or via Malay kecap (phonetically kətʃap) 'fish sauce,' from Southern Min (Chinese dialects of southeast Fujian) kôe-chiap (Xiamen), kê-chiap (Zhangzhou), from kôe, kê 'salted or pickled fish or shellfish' + chiap 'juice, sap'”. Its definition: ketchup is “usually made from tomatoes”.
Tycoon comes from Japanese 'taikun' “great lord”, a title of the shogun used with foreigners, from Chinese 大 “great” + 君 “lord” (Mandarin dà jūn).
facts.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, 'tycoon', https://www.etymonline.com/word/tycoon (checked from search snippet)

facts.text: Typhoon comes mainly from Arabic 'tufan', shaped by Greek 'Typhon'; “Chinese (Cantonese) tai fung 'a great wind' also might have influenced the form or sense of the word in English”. So the video says Chinese may have shaped it, not that it is the origin.
facts.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, 'typhoon', https://www.etymonline.com/word/typhoon (checked from search snippet)

facts.text: In Greek myth Typhon (Typhoeus) is a monster the storm winds come from. Quoted: "And from Typhoeus come boisterous winds which blow damply" (lines 869–870); he had "a hundred heads of a snake, a fearful dragon" (lines 824–825) and is called "the monster" (line 856).
facts.source: Hesiod, Theogony, tr. H. G. Evelyn-White 1914, Perseus Digital Library, Tufts University, https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.01.0130:card=853

facts.text: Kowtow comes from Chinese k'o-t'ou 叩頭, “knock” + “head”: touching the forehead to the ground while kneeling.
facts.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, 'kowtow', https://www.etymonline.com/word/kowtow (checked from search snippet)

shots.title: Hook: four words
shots.show: Four-word stack: KETCHUP, TYCOON, TYPHOON, KOWTOW slam in one by one, huge, white, filling the frame top to bottom. A big '4' in fire orange rolls up from 1 to 4 beside the stack as each word lands, then an orange marker sweeps across the whole stack.
shots.motion: Each word drops in from above with a short squash bounce (one every 0.5 s), the counter ticks with them, the marker sweep finishes at 3 s and the stack shakes lightly.

shots.title: Ketchup
shots.show: Word card: KETCHUP lands huge at the top in white. Below it the Chinese root 'kê-chiap' (Southern Min, i.e. Hokkien) rises in amber. Then the line 'Started as tomato sauce' types in word by word; 'tomato' is struck through in red and rolls into 'pickled fish', which gets an orange marker sweep. A simple fish icon swims across the empty lower third and a tomato icon fades in last, small, labelled 'today' (today's ketchup is usually made from tomatoes).
shots.text: Ketchup began as a fish sauce
shots.motion: Word pops, root rises from below, line types, strike-through draws left to right, the struck word rolls vertically like a slot reel into the right one, marker sweeps, fish swims continuously.

shots.title: Tycoon
shots.show: Word card, same layout: the Chinese characters 大君 land at the top in amber with 'great + lord' under them. An arrow hop path runs down through 'taikun (Japanese)' to TYCOON landing huge in white. Then 'boss' appears struck through beside it and rolls into 'great lord', with the orange marker sweep. A small crown icon drops onto the last O.
shots.text: Tycoon: 'great lord', by way of Japanese
shots.motion: Characters stamp in, the arrow draws down hop by hop, each stop lights as reached, TYCOON slams in, the strike-and-roll, crown drops with a bounce.

shots.title: Typhoon
shots.show: Word card, same layout: the word's main roots slide in from left and right: 'tufan' (Arabic) and 'Typhon' (Greek, 'storm monster'), both cooler grey. They collide in the middle and fuse into TYPHOON, huge and white. Wind streaks whip across the frame behind the type and the letters wobble in the gusts. Then the Chinese part, as a maybe, in the lower third: 大風 in amber, tagged 'Cantonese · may have shaped it', with 'tai fung, 'a great wind'' under it and an orange marker sweep; a small wind icon beside it.
shots.text: Typhoon: Arabic, Greek, and maybe Chinese
shots.motion: Roots slide in from opposite sides, merge with a flash, TYPHOON spins in a quarter turn and settles, wind particles stream left to right for the whole shot.
shots.source: Etymonline, 'typhoon' (mainly Arabic tufan and Greek Typhon; Cantonese tai fung may have influenced it)

shots.title: Kowtow
shots.show: Word card, same layout: 叩頭 lands in amber, then splits into two halves labelled 'knock' and 'head'. KOWTOW lands huge in white; the whole word bows forward until its top touches a ground line, then straightens. Orange marker sweeps under 'knock head'.
shots.motion: Characters stamp, split apart with a tick, the English word tilts forward like a bow (twice, slow), dust puff where it touches the line, marker sweep.

shots.title: End card
shots.show: Four-word stack returns exactly as in shot 1 (same order, size and white type), now each word carries its small amber root beside it: fish sauce, great lord, great wind? (hedged: Chinese may only have shaped typhoon), knock head. A stamp 'SHAPED BY CHINESE' lands across the stack in fire orange.
shots.motion: Roots pop in one after another down the stack, the stamp slams with a short shake, a slow drift zoom keeps the frame moving to the end.
